name: Sous Vide Pork Chops
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt presents this as a complete guide rather than a single recipe, aimed at the reader who grew up on dry, overcooked chops. Because the water bath sits at the temperature you actually want to serve, the chop cooks evenly from edge to edge and timing becomes forgiving, so the choice of temperature does all the work: he walks through the texture at 130F, 140F, 150F and 160F and picks 140F as his own favourite for meat that is juicy but still has a meaty bite. Time still matters at the margins, and he caps the bath at about four hours before the muscle fibres go mushy. Brining is unnecessary, bone-in chops gain flavour that spreads through the meat in a sealed bag, and because sous vide cannot brown anything, the chop has to be finished fast in a smoking-hot skillet or over a hot grill.
comment_digest: The most repeated safety note warns against putting fresh garlic in the bag at bath temperatures below 140F, citing the anaerobic environment and C. botulinum. Results at 140F split sharply: one cook calls 140F for 90 minutes on a two-inch bone-in chop perfect, while another found a one-inch-plus chop at the same setting practically inedible. A detailed troubleshooting comment aimed at those failures blames the finish rather than the bath, advising thick bone-in chops, a smoking pan with avocado rather than olive oil, a sear measured in seconds not minutes, and no resting at all, which contradicts the recipe's three-to-five-minute rest. One reader flags an apparent conflict between the fifteen-minutes-per-half-inch rule of thumb and the chart's flat one-to-four-hour range. Several readers ask whether chops chilled in an ice bath can simply be seared the next day; none of those questions are answered in the visible text.
flags: Comments are heavily truncated at 'Read More'. A large share of the review section is unanswered reader questions rather than feedback. The star rating is based on 13 ratings while 45 reviews are listed.
